name: Victor Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the service department of a big brand dealership out on the ring road, twelve bays, all shiny floors and blue lights. I get my jobs on a tablet, plug the car into the diagnostic laptop, and then it's servicing, recalls and warranty work, mostly cars under five years old. We're paid on flat rate, so if the book says a water pump is two hours and I do it in ninety minutes, I get the two hours. What wears me out is when a job goes wrong, a seized bolt or a missing part, and the clock keeps ticking while I'm earning nothing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel about the place, and who's around you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's decent, honestly, and the union got us a proper pay deal two years ago, which is why I'm a member. My mate Gaz works the bay next to me and we eat lunch in his van because the canteen is grim. I live with my girlfriend Priya, who drives buses, and we've got about four months of bills put away. I use one of those AI chat apps now and then, mostly to make sense of a weird wiring diagram.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: decent tools, lots of hype. At work I'd joke that the AI could finally write Gaz's job notes for him, because his handwriting on the tablet is somehow still awful. Online I'd say nothing, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, flat rate is my real problem, not AI. The book times get trimmed every year by the manufacturer, and a slow week means a thin payslip. Priya and I are trying to save for a deposit, and a bad month knocks us back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep paying into the union. I'd ask my rep to push for a guaranteed minimum on flat rate in the next pay talks. And I'd keep putting 250 a month into the deposit pot, like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit of a grumble in the background about pay, but nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the book times get trimmed every year. What does a bad month actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last February I had a week where half my jobs were waiting on parts from Germany. I clocked twenty-six paid hours in a forty-hour week. That's a few hundred quid gone, and that's the month the car insurance renewal landed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the AI tools you use now make any difference to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, maybe. If the AI could chase parts and tell me which jobs to start first, I'd waste less time. But the dealer would probably just trim the book times again to take the savings.

say: I'd say it's **what I expected**: decent tools and a lot of hype.
I'd joke that AI could finally **write Gaz's notes**, but wouldn't post anything online.
think: **Flat-rate pay** is my real problem, because book times get trimmed every year.
A slow week means a **thin payslip** and sets back our house deposit.
do: Keep working the dealership bays and **stay in the union**.
Ask the union rep for a **guaranteed minimum** on flat rate at the next talks.
Keep putting **250 a month** into the deposit savings with Priya.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a background grumble about pay.
S0.quote: Flat rate is my real problem, not AI. The book times get trimmed every year by the manufacturer, and a slow week means a thin payslip.
fieldNote: His stress is **pay structure**, not technology; flat rate shifts the risk onto him.
Expects any time saved by AI to be **taken by the dealer**, not shared.
Concrete memory of a **26-hour week** waiting on parts.

steps.text: Ask the union rep to push for a flat-rate minimum in pay talks
Keep paying 250 a month into the house deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the union at the table before the dealer brings any of it in. Stuff like who keeps the hours when the AI cuts the time a job takes. I'd say it in the canteen, and I'd go to the branch meeting, which I usually skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the dealer is exactly where this hits first. The service advisers, the parts desk, the warranty claims clerk, that's all thinking work, and the manufacturer will push AI straight into it. For me, the AI tells me the fault before I open the bonnet, the book time drops, and I'm still paid by the book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI diagnostic stuff properly, not just now and then, because if it's coming I'd rather be the one who knows it. I'd go on the high-voltage course the dealer offers, since electric cars are what's left of the real work. And I'd get properly involved in the union, maybe stand as a workplace rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not helpless. There's something to do about it, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra on the parts desk, straight away. She's been there twenty years, she knows every part number in her head, and that's exactly what an AI does in a second. I'd want the union fighting to move people like Sandra somewhere, not just pay them off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand as a rep. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, mostly, and a bit of the managers' goodwill. The reps get the rubbish jobs sometimes, the ones that never pay the book time. I'd still do it, because nobody else under forty will.

say: I'd say the **union** must be at the table before the dealer brings AI in.
I'd argue about **who keeps the hours** when AI cuts job times, and attend branch meetings.
think: The dealer's **desk jobs** — advisers, parts, warranty — get hit first.
AI finds faults faster, the **book time drops**, and I'm still paid by the book.
do: Use the **AI diagnostic tools** properly instead of only now and then.
Take the dealer's **high-voltage course** for electric cars.
Stand as a **workplace union rep** in the first year.
feel: **Nervous but not helpless**, because there are things he can do.
S1.quote: AI tells me the fault before I open the bonnet, the book time drops, and I'm still paid by the book.
fieldNote: He sees clearly how **flat rate** turns AI's speed into his pay cut.
Worries about **Sandra on parts**, a 20-year colleague doing pure thinking work.
Willing to pay a cost in **managers' goodwill** to become a rep.

steps.text: Use the dealer's AI diagnostic software on every job
Complete the dealer's high-voltage electric car course
Stand for election as the workplace union rep

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in, full stop: a tax on the companies doing it and a wage for the people it hits. I'd say it loudly, at work and at the union branch. I'd probably even post for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the dealership is finished as a place to work for someone like me within a few years. The car diagnoses itself and orders its own parts by 2028, and then by 2031 the manufacturer puts robot arms in the bays. They already love a clean, controlled workshop, so a dealer is the easiest place on earth to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Priya the first weekend and stop the deposit plan, and keep that money as a cushion instead. I'd get out of the dealer within the first year and into an independent garage, where the work is older, messier cars. And I'd push the union hard for a deal on redundancy pay before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. Angry too, because nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stopping the deposit plan feel like for you and Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful, honestly. We'd been looking at a two-bed near her depot. But I'd rather rent for longer than buy a house in 2028 and lose my job in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would an independent garage be safer than the dealer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots will be built for clean bays and new cars with all the data. A twelve-year-old van with rust and someone's bodge job under it is a nightmare for a machine. It buys me time, maybe not forever.

say: I'd say the **government** must step in with a tax on AI firms and a wage for those hit.
I'd say it at work and at the branch, and probably **post online** for once.
think: A dealership is the **easiest place** on earth to automate, with clean bays and data.
Cars diagnose themselves by 2028 and **robot arms** reach the bays by 2031.
do: Pause the **house deposit** with Priya and keep it as a cushion.
Move to an **independent garage** with older, messier cars within a year.
Push the union for a **redundancy deal** before the robots arrive.
feel: **Properly scared**, and angry that nobody voted for this.
S2.quote: I'd rather rent for longer than buy a house in 2028 and lose my job in 2031.
fieldNote: He links the **three-year robot gap** directly to his housing decision.
Sees **messy old cars** as a refuge from machines built for clean bays.
Shifts from tweaking pay deals to **demanding a wage** for those displaced.

steps.text: Pause the two-bed house deposit and keep the money as a cushion
Move from the dealership to an independent garage within a year
Push the union for a redundancy deal before robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd say the union and the government both need a plan by next year, not in 2030. I'd be pushing for retraining money tied to the companies that profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is the difference between panic and a plan for me. I'd be thirty-two when AGI hits, and the dealer's thinking jobs go then, but my hands-on bit lasts till about 2034. That's seven years of work, which is a whole career change if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the deposit plan, but go for a cheaper place and a smaller mortgage. I'd do the high-voltage course and then look at training as a technician who maintains the robots and charging kit, not the cars. And I'd keep the union work going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but a bit motivated, oddly. Like the start of a hard season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd train to maintain robots. Do you know what that job actually looks like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, if I'm honest. I imagine it's like what I do now, just the patient is a machine arm instead of a car. I'd want to talk to whoever already does it at the factory up the road before I spent money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Priya, how does her bus job fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buses are probably going driverless at some point too, and that's scary. So we'd both be planning at once, which is either a nightmare or good teamwork. I'd say teamwork, most days.

say: I'd say we've got **five years**, so plans are needed by next year, not 2030.
I'd push for **retraining money** paid for by the companies that profit.
think: Five years is the difference between **panic and a plan** for me.
My hands-on work lasts **till about 2034**, enough time for a career change.
do: Buy a **cheaper place** with a smaller mortgage instead of dropping the deposit.
Train toward **maintaining robots** and charging kit after the high-voltage course.
Keep up **union work** on retraining money.
feel: **Worried but motivated**, like the start of a hard season.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between panic and a plan for me.
fieldNote: He uses the **2034 robot date** to count seven working years left.
Admits he **doesn't know** what robot maintenance work involves yet.
Both incomes are exposed: **Priya's bus job** may automate too.

steps.text: Buy a smaller place near Priya's depot with a lower mortgage
Train as a technician maintaining robots and charging equipment
Keep pushing the union for company-funded retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly if anyone in charge bothers. I'd be voting on it and saying so at the union. Plenty of warning, so no excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-seven when AGI lands and forty when the robots come. That's a lot of runway. I'd probably be a workshop foreman or out of the dealer by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house with Priya as planned and carry on. I'd keep learning the AI tools as they come into the dealer, which they would. Then maybe in five or six years, I'd decide whether to move into robot maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, actually. Uneasy for other people more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry for other people. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older lads, the ones in their fifties who'll be sixty-odd when the robots come. Too young to retire, too old for anyone to retrain properly. I'd want the union looking after them first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy the house now. Isn't that a risk if the work goes by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but I'd have twelve years of mortgage paid by then, and Priya and I both working. You can't stop living for ten years because of a date. We'd just get a smaller mortgage than the bank offers.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so there's no excuse for an unfair change.
I'd **vote** on it and push the union to plan early.
think: At **forty** when robots arrive, I have plenty of runway.
I'd likely be a **foreman** or out of the dealer by then anyway.
do: Buy the house with Priya as planned, with a **smaller mortgage** than offered.
Learn new **AI tools** as the dealer brings them in.
Decide in five or six years whether to **retrain** into robot maintenance.
feel: **Okay**, and uneasy more for older colleagues than for himself.
S4.quote: You can't stop living for ten years because of a date.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into **ordinary planning**.
His concern shifts to **colleagues in their fifties**, too old to retrain easily.
Still trims risk with a **smaller mortgage**, a sign he isn't fully relaxed.

steps.text: Buy the house with Priya on a smaller mortgage than offered
Learn each new AI tool as the dealership brings it in
Vote for parties planning fair retraining for older workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because the dealer would go first and the house plan would die with it. What would help is a union deal that says nobody gets binned without a year's pay and paid retraining. And honest information about which jobs are coming, so I'm not guessing from the news.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about flat rate, really, and that's the bit that matters for mechanics. Speed turns into a pay cut for us. Every minute the AI saves a flat-rate mechanic is a minute the dealer stops paying for.

headlineQuote: Every minute the AI saves a flat-rate mechanic is a minute the dealer stops paying for.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old dealership mechanic** paid on flat rate, living with his girlfriend Priya, a bus driver.
He uses AI apps **now and then** and adopts tools once they're proven.
A union member, he turns each scenario into a question of **who keeps the hours**.
His mood runs from **uneasy to alarmed**, with the two-year AGI case killing their house plan.
Ten years of warning lets him **plan calmly** and worry more for older colleagues.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the dealership automates first and their house plan collapses.
whatWouldHelp: A union deal guaranteeing **a year's pay** and paid retraining for anyone let go.
Honest **information** on which jobs are going, rather than guessing from the news.
